text.title: Growth Referral Programs Failure Modes
text.summary: Six antipatterns observed when applying Growth Referral Programs. Each pairs symptom + root-cause + concrete fix. Detector clauses make them mechanically catchable.

antipattern.symptom: Referral sign-ups spike; almost none purchase; reward credits balloon; the top ten referrers share a payment card.

root-cause.source: Widely established practice in referral fraud prevention

antipattern.root-cause: The qualifying event was account creation, so every throwaway account was paid.
antipattern.fix: Enforce rule `r-reward-on-qualifying-event-not-signup`: release rewards only on a paid order above a minimum or a real activation milestone, held until the refund window closes.

antipattern.symptom: Dozens of referees share the referrer's device fingerprint or a plus-addressed variant of the referrer's email; rewards were paid, and paid again after a queue retry.

root-cause.source: templates/k_factor.py notes; widely established practice in referral fraud prevention

antipattern.root-cause: No match on payment instrument, device, IP or normalised email; reward fulfilment was not idempotent.
antipattern.fix: Enforce rule `r-fraud-guard-self-referral-and-idempotent-rewards`: self-referral matching before reward release, one reward per (referrer_id, referee_id, qualifying_event) tuple.

antipattern.symptom: The spec projects K of 0.9 from 30 invites in the beta; at scale K reads 0.15; headcount was planned on the first number.
antipattern.root-cause: K was computed below the sample floor and presented without cycle time or reward cost.
antipattern.fix: Enforce rule `r-k-factor-computed-on-500-plus-invites`: no K reported below 500 invites and 50 referrers; present K below 1 as the 1 / (1 - K) multiplier net of reward cost.

antipattern.symptom: The share prompt sits on the welcome screen; share rate is under 1 percent; users who do share send invitations that never convert.

root-cause.source: Dropbox and Airbnb referral programme case studies (widely cited)

antipattern.root-cause: No trigger event was defined, so the prompt fired at sign-up when the user had nothing to recommend yet.
antipattern.fix: Enforce rule `r-trigger-event-at-value-moment`: fire the prompt on a named value event and record what share of users reach it.

antipattern.symptom: "$20 give, $20 get" on a $30 average first order; every successful referral loses money; finance discovers it at quarter close via credit liabilities.
antipattern.root-cause: The incentive was copied from a famous programme with different unit economics; no per-referee cost versus CAC and margin check was recorded.
antipattern.fix: Enforce rule `r-double-sided-incentive-within-unit-economics`: reward per qualified referee at or below paid CAC and a stated fraction of first-order margin or LTV, shown in the spec.

antipattern.symptom: Referees sign up on a different device than the one that opened the link; referrers complain of unpaid rewards; reported K undercounts and nobody trusts the programme numbers.

root-cause.source: Widely established practice in referral programme operations

antipattern.root-cause: The referral was tracked as `utm_source=referral` in analytics; no per-user code was persisted server-side at account creation.
antipattern.fix: Enforce rule `r-referral-attribution-server-side`: unique per-user code or link, first-party cookie or code entry at sign-up, and the link stored on the referee account.

section.title: Human checkpoint
section.p: Before any binding action driven by a Growth Referral Programs output (launching the programme, changing reward amounts, sending lifecycle emails, releasing held rewards), a named human reviewer must sign off. The agent surfaces a `ready_for_review=true` flag and does NOT auto-commit decisions, copy, configs, or rollouts.
